title: 3.6.7 Plain English to Pseudocode: Reassignment vs. Mutation Trace
description: Turn plain-English steps into pseudocode for process(nums): one write mutates the shared array and the caller sees it, the other reassigns the local name and the caller does not.

steps.title: Turn the plain-English steps into pseudocode
steps.instructions:
Here is the plan in plain English. The caller has `scores = [10, 20, 30]` and calls `process(scores)`, so inside the function `nums` is a second name for the same array.

**1.** Set item 0 of `nums` to 0.

**2.** Ask: did the caller see that? Yes, because `nums` and `scores` are the same array, so `scores` now starts with 0.

**3.** Point `nums` at a brand new array, `[9, 9]`.

**4.** Ask: did the caller see that? No, only the local name moved, so `scores` is unchanged.

**5.** Back in the caller, `scores` prints as `[0, 20, 30]`.

The same plan is drawn as a flow chart above the editor (open the Flow Chart bar). You do not draw it, you read it: the first diamond answers yes, the second answers no, and both paths meet at one print.

In `README.md`, type these as numbered pseudocode **between the first and last line**. Number every line, including indented ones. Each keyword looks like this, in a different program:

- `SET item 1 OF list TO 5` (change one item in an array)
- `SET list TO a NEW array` (point a name somewhere else)
- `ASK did the caller see this? YES: ...` (a question and its answer)
- `OUTPUT list` (show the result)

Plain English is fine here. Press **Grade** above the editor: the AI reads what your steps mean and marks each Quest card green or red. Changing your text clears its marks, so press Grade again when you have finished editing.

Before you submit, run the code in your head: the 0 survives in `scores`, and the `[9, 9]` never leaves the function.
hints: Two writes, two questions: the first answer is yes (one shared array), the second is no (only the local name moved).
The last line should say what the caller prints, and it is not [9, 9].

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your steps
aiCheck.prompt: The student was given plain-English steps and rewrote them as numbered, step-by-step pseudocode in README.md, between a first line and a last line that were already there. The program they were describing is process(nums): the caller has scores = [10, 20, 30] and calls process(scores). Inside, nums and scores name the same array. Step 1 sets item 0 of nums to 0 (a mutation of the shared array, so the caller sees it). Step 2 points nums at a brand new array [9, 9] (a reassignment of the local name only, so the caller does not see it). The caller then prints scores as 0, 20, 30. Judge each criterion ONLY by whether its idea is present in the student's steps, however they word it. Plain English, keywords such as SET, IF, END IF, RETURN, or a mix of both are all fine, and so are different names, different capitalisation, and different ways to number the lines. Do not require any particular keyword. A step that is clearly aimed at the criterion is enough for 'met'. Mark a criterion 'missing' only when the idea is absent or the steps do the opposite, for example saying the caller sees the [9, 9] array for the reassignment criterion. Write each note for THIS student's own steps: in a not-met note, name the exact step or word in their steps that causes the problem (quote at most a few words), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected steps. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their steps satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.
